title: Localism and the Tirocinium Militiae
author: Michael Foster
summary: Michael Foster argues that biblical localism -- giving first priority to the people and places God has set before you -- is not inconsistent with temporary departures. Drawing on his own experience leaving Cincinnati for five years in South Carolina before returning to plant roots and build a family estate, he distinguishes between rootlessness (drift) and temporary mobility (mission). The ancient Roman concept of tirocinium militiae -- the 'apprenticeship of military service' -- represents a cultural expectation that men be shaped through proving grounds: hardship, responsibility, submission to authority, before being trusted with leadership. Ancient households were 'oriented around return, not permanent departure.' Modern society has largely inverted this, treating departure as the default and rootedness as optional. Foster argues that healthy homelands produce men who can leave for a season, return with greater wisdom and provision, and strengthen the people and place they love.
points: * Biblical localism means 'giving first priority to the people and place God has put directly in front of you' -- but over a lifetime those people and places can legitimately shift. * Tirocinium militiae (Latin: 'apprenticeship of military service') described the formative period when a young man was shaped by hardship and duty before being trusted with authority -- applicable beyond warfare. * 'There is a difference between being rootless and being temporarily mobile so that you can eventually become deeply rooted. One is drift. The other is mission.' * Ancient households were 'oriented around return, not permanent departure' -- exile was a severe punishment because permanent separation from household, land, and people was social death. * Modern society has inverted the ancient default: 'Ancient people treated rootedness as the norm and departure as the exception that needed a reason. Modern society mostly assumes the reverse.' * Foster's tour of duty in South Carolina was essential preparation -- not contradiction -- for his eventual deep rootedness on the east side of Cincinnati.
quotes: There is a difference between being rootless and being temporarily mobile so that you can eventually become deeply rooted. One is drift. The other is mission.

A healthy homeland should produce men who can go out into the world without forgetting where they came from, and who can return, if God wills, with greater wisdom and provision for the people they love.
The wandering was meant to serve the settling.

One of the great differences between the modern world and the ancient world is that older societies expected young men to pass through some sort of tirocinium militiae before being trusted with authority.
Ancient people did not treat those things as optional accessories. They were bound together.
